turns.t: Good morning, doctor. Nothing to report, really, I'm only here because the letter said it was time for the pacemaker check.
That's the best sort of visit. Have you had any symptoms at all since I saw you last?
Not a thing, really. Well, I get a bit tired going up the hill by the church, but at my age I'd expect that.
Fair enough. No dizzy spells or blackouts? ~
None. I'd have told you. I'm very good at telling people things. Ask my wife. ~
Let me check your pulse and blood pressure first. ~
Go on. ~
Pulse 62 and regular, blood pressure 130 over 78.
Is that all right? ~
Very good. I've already checked your pacemaker with the programmer this morning, before you came in.
Did it hurt? ~
You weren't even here. The device has been talking to the machine since eight.
Clever things. And what did it say? ~
The battery has about six years left, the wires are working properly, and the heart rhythm is well controlled. ~
Six years. I'll be ninety. ~
I'll still be here, I hope, or my successor will. ~
Do I need to do anything differently? ~
Not at all. Carry on as you are, keep walking up the church hill, it's good for you. ~
I do the hill every Sunday. ~
Splendid. Just remember to carry your pacemaker card, and tell any dentist or surgeon you've got one. ~
I carry it everywhere. ~
And mobile phones are fine, just don't keep one in your breast pocket over the device. ~
In my trouser pocket, always. ~
Perfect. ~
Will I be seeing you again? ~
The pacemaker clinic will send you the next date. But if you have dizziness, a faint, a very slow pulse, or your chest muscle twitches, don't wait, ring us.
I'll ring straight away. ~
Lovely. Thank you for coming, and give my regards to your wife. ~
I will. She'll be pleased to hear I passed. ~
With flying colours. ~
